nodes.milestone: Deliver a mathematical document and a standard-library command-line checker, obtained from the public repository with one documented command and a real recorded run. For positive integers a,b,c, let T have one centre and three paths of a,b,c further vertices. Prove disjoint equal-size subsets with identical multisets of all pairwise distances, each of size at least floor((1+a+b+c)/2)-1, or give an infinite structural obstruction family with a rigorous upper bound refuting that target. First independently reconstruct the published cases, fixing endpoints explicitly, and refresh priority. A signed distance-shell formulation may guide the work; it is not an algorithmic or mathematical result already delivered. No gallery simulation or finite census substitutes for the proof. Acceptance: A non-author reconstructs the argument for every length and parity class and writes an independent distance counter for fresh unequal triples. They verify disjointness, size and multiplicities, and ensure a deliberately altered pair is rejected. For a negative family they audit the upper bound over every permitted pair, not just failed search branches. Drop for a missed case, an unsupported endpoint repair, prior resolution, only finite experiments, or a result about isometry instead of equal distance multisets. Priority must be stated provisionally until the unread sources are resolved.
nodes.plain: Can almost all dots on three paths meeting at one junction be split into two equal groups with exactly the same distance counts? A proof would answer a concrete question about branching networks.

nodes.first_version: Ship a Python experiment library, three executable resource-owning workloads, a finite controlled policy experiment and a concise results paper. Start with weighted job admission, then fan-out cleanup and interrupted multi-step work. Each workload has an independently written ownership oracle and a native asyncio witness; additional runtime adapters require ordinary dependency approval. nodes.benefit: Library authors gain runnable evidence about which cancellation guarantees their resource-ownership protocol needs. The deliverable shows lost or duplicated work, leaked capacity and recovery behavior under declared conditions, so a maintainer can choose or repair a protocol without treating all async runtimes as interchangeable.
nodes.interest: A Design Space Exploration of Async/Await already supplies the core models and native differential testing, but explicitly asks whether simultaneous cancellation prevents realistic bugs that bottom-up cancellation permits. Bryan C. Mills gives a concrete semaphore-ownership problem on Async-SIG. AnyIO documents why repeated cancellation changes cleanup behavior. These establish a research question, not a promised answer.
nodes.check: Before experimentation, a non-author agrees the invariant and verifies that the controlled comparison changes only the named cancellation rule, keeping persistence and start-of-task behavior fixed. They rerun the frozen workload set, reconstruct one loss and one successful recovery, and check native witnesses separately. A negative or mixed result is valid. Drop the project if confounding cannot be removed, if the cases merely restate the existing paper, or if no application-level ownership consequence beyond known examples is established. No universal safety or performance ranking is promised.
nodes.reach: The primary audience is the seven runtime communities compared by the paper and the maintainers of resource-owning async libraries. The first executable case serves the Python resource-pool problem already described publicly. This is plausibly several teams and tens of specialists; readership, adoption and general bug prevalence have not been measured.
nodes.rather: A carefully controlled result about cancellation and resource ownership could affect libraries used beyond this house. That warrants several weeks more than another room control only if the first gate isolates a real policy trade-off. It is not justified by reproducing the paper or collecting ordinary timeout bugs; those are explicit rejection conditions.

nodes.title: When Cancellation Loses Work
nodes.what: Answer the open empirical question in A Design Space Exploration of Async/Await: which cancellation rules prevent realistic bugs? Build a reproducible corpus of resource-owning programs, an importable experiment harness, controlled policy comparisons and native-runtime witnesses. Study weighted job admission, fan-out cleanup and interrupted multi-step work. nodes.why: Gray, Krishnamurthi and Crichton already provide executable semantics and a native differential fuzzer. Their paper explicitly leaves realistic cancellation trade-offs open. The Async-SIG semaphore discussion supplies one concrete resource-ownership problem; AnyIO documents a distinct cancellation policy. What is missing to establish is controlled evidence about application protocols, not another model of the same core semantics.
nodes.first_step: Preregister the first resource-ownership invariant, cancellation timing bounds and comparison before running experiments. Use the semaphore-admission case to establish that one policy axis can be changed while workload, cleanup protocol, cancellation persistence and all other rules stay fixed. Stop if the apparent difference only comes from unmatched runtimes or a known bug with no policy consequence.
